module_title: Choosing and Preparing Rootstocks for African Conditions

lessons.title: Selecting rootstocks for drought tolerance in semi-arid areas
lessons.body:
In semi-arid Africa, choosing the right rootstock is the difference between a mango tree that survives and one that dies in the first dry season. Drought-tolerant rootstocks have deep taproots and thick bark that reduces water loss. For mango, local varieties like 'Dodo' or 'Kenya' are known for drought tolerance. For citrus, rough lemon (Citrus jambhiri) and Troyer citrange are good choices. Avocado is less drought-tolerant, but 'Duke 7' and 'Zutano' rootstocks handle dry spells better than most.

Start by testing your soil. Dig a hole 60 cm deep and 30 cm wide. Fill it with water. If it drains within 24 hours, you have good drainage. If not, choose rootstocks that tolerate occasional waterlogging, like rough lemon. In dry areas, plant on raised beds or ridges to capture water. Space trees 8-10 meters apart for mango, 5-7 meters for citrus, and 6-8 meters for avocado.

Collect seeds from local, healthy mother trees that have survived at least 10 years of local droughts. Avoid seeds from irrigated orchardsâthey may lack drought-hardiness. For mango, use polyembryonic seeds (they produce multiple seedlings, one of which is a clone). For citrus, extract seeds from ripe fruit, wash them, and plant within 24 hours; they lose viability quickly.

Plant seeds in nursery beds or polythene tubes filled with a mix of 3 parts soil, 2 parts sand, and 1 part compost. Water daily for the first month, then reduce to every 2-3 days. In dry areas, mulch around seedlings with dry grass to keep moisture. After 3-4 months, seedlings are ready for grafting. Remember: a drought-tolerant rootstock does not make the tree immune to droughtâyou still need to water young trees during dry spells.

lessons.title: Growing rootstocks from local seeds: mango, avocado, citrus
lessons.body:
Growing your own rootstocks from local seeds saves money and ensures the rootstock is adapted to your area. Start with fresh, healthy seeds from mature trees. For mango, choose seeds from polyembryonic varieties like 'Dodo' or 'Kenya'âthese produce multiple seedlings, and you can use the strongest one as rootstock. For avocado, use seeds from local varieties like 'Fuerte' or 'Hass' that have grown well in your region. For citrus, rough lemon or local sweet orange seeds work well.

Extract seeds carefully. For mango, remove the husk and plant the seed immediatelyâit loses viability in a few days. For avocado, remove the seed coat and plant pointed end up, about 2 cm deep. For citrus, wash seeds to remove sugar and plant within 24 hours. Plant in nursery beds or black polythene tubes (20 cm x 10 cm) filled with a mix of 3 parts loam soil, 2 parts river sand, and 1 part well-rotted manure. Water daily.

Germination takes 2-4 weeks for mango, 3-6 weeks for avocado, and 2-3 weeks for citrus. Keep seedlings in partial shade for the first month, then gradually expose them to full sun. Thin mango seedlings: keep only the strongest one per pot. For avocado, pinch the tip when the seedling is 30 cm tall to encourage a thick stem. For citrus, remove any thorns or side shoots below 20 cm.

Feed seedlings with a weak solution of NPK 20-10-10 every two weeks. Watch for pests like aphids and whitefliesâspray with soapy water (1 tablespoon liquid soap per litre) if needed. After 4-6 months, seedlings should be 40-60 cm tall with a stem diameter of 0.5-0.8 cmâready for grafting. Always label your seedlings with the seed source and date.

lessons.title: When and how to transplant rootstocks into nursery beds
lessons.body:
Transplanting rootstocks into nursery beds gives them more space to grow strong before grafting. The best time is at the start of the rainy season, when soil is moist and temperatures are moderate. In East Africa, this is March-April or October-November. Avoid transplanting in hot, dry monthsâseedlings will suffer shock.

Prepare the nursery bed two weeks in advance. Choose a site with full sun and good drainage. Clear all weeds and dig the soil 30 cm deep. Mix in 2 buckets of well-rotted manure per square meter. Make beds 1 meter wide and 10-15 cm high, and any length you need. Space seedlings 20 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart. This gives each rootstock enough room for a strong root system.

Water the seedlings in their tubes or seedbed thoroughly before lifting. Use a hand fork or small spade to lift them with a ball of soil around the roots. Avoid pulling by the stemâhold by a leaf. Plant at the same depth as before. Firm the soil around the roots and water immediately. Mulch with dry grass to conserve moisture.

After transplanting, shade the seedlings with a simple shade net or palm fronds for the first week. Water every morning for the first two weeks, then every 2-3 days. Remove any weeds by handâdo not use herbicides. After one month, the seedlings should be established. Continue watering and feeding with a weak NPK solution every two weeks. Rootstocks are ready for grafting when they are 6-12 months old, depending on species. Mango: 6-8 months; avocado: 8-12 months; citrus: 6-10 months. Always keep records of transplanting date and seedling source.

lessons.title: Preparing rootstock seedlings for grafting: size, age, and health
lessons.body:
Grafting success depends on the rootstock being at the right stage. For mango, the rootstock should be 6-8 months old, with a stem diameter of 0.8-1.2 cm (about the thickness of a pencil). For avocado, 8-12 months, stem diameter 0.6-1.0 cm. For citrus, 6-10 months, stem diameter 0.5-0.8 cm. Measure at 10 cm above the soil line. If too thin, wait; if too thick, the graft may not take.

The rootstock must be healthy: no pests, no disease, and actively growing. Check for signs of stress: yellow leaves, wilting, or stunted growth. If you see aphids, whiteflies, or scales, treat with soapy water (1 tablespoon liquid soap per litre) or neem oil (5 ml per litre). Remove any diseased seedlings immediately.

Two weeks before grafting, water the rootstocks well but do not fertilizeâhigh nitrogen can cause excessive sap flow and reduce graft success. On the day of grafting, the rootstock should be well-watered. Use a clean, sharp grafting knife. Sterilize the blade with alcohol or a flame between cuts. Make a clean cut at 10-15 cm above the soil. The cut should be smooth and flat.

For a wedge graft, cut the rootstock stem at a 45-degree angle, then make a vertical slit 2-3 cm deep. For a side graft, make a slanting cut 3-4 cm long. The scion (the top part) must be from a known good variety, collected from a healthy mother tree, and matched in diameter to the rootstock. Wrap the graft union tightly with grafting tape or polythene strips. Cover with a plastic bag to retain humidity. Keep in shade for 2-3 weeks. After 3 weeks, check for new growthâif the scion is green, the graft has taken. Remove the tape after 4-6 weeks.

lessons.title: Managing rootstock pests and diseases without expensive chemicals
lessons.body:
Rootstock seedlings are vulnerable to pests and diseases, but you don't need expensive chemicals. Start with prevention: keep the nursery clean, remove weeds, and space seedlings well for airflow. Water at the base, not on leaves, to reduce fungal diseases. Rotate nursery beds if possible.

Common pests: aphids, whiteflies, mealybugs, and scales. For aphids and whiteflies, spray with soapy water: mix 1 tablespoon of liquid soap (not detergent) in 1 litre of water. Spray in the evening, covering the undersides of leaves. Repeat every 3 days for two weeks. For mealybugs, use a cotton swab dipped in alcohol to remove them, or spray with neem oil (5 ml per litre of water). For scales, scrape them off with a soft brush, then spray with soapy water.

Common diseases: damping-off (fungal), powdery mildew, and root rot. Damping-off causes seedlings to collapse at the soil line. Prevent by using well-drained soil and not overwatering. If it appears, remove affected seedlings and drench soil with a weak solution of baking soda (1 teaspoon per litre). Powdery mildew shows as white powder on leaves. Spray with a mix of 1 tablespoon baking soda and 1 teaspoon liquid soap in 1 litre of water. Root rot causes yellowing and wilting. Improve drainage and avoid waterlogging. Remove severely affected plants.

For bacterial diseases like citrus canker, there is no cheap cure. Prevent by using clean seed and tools. Sterilize pruning tools with alcohol. Remove and burn infected plants. Always inspect new seedlings before bringing them into the nursery. Keep a log of pest and disease outbreaks, and which treatments worked. Share this with other farmers.

lessons.title: Hands-on: Selecting and preparing 10 rootstocks for grafting
lessons.body:
In this practical session, you will select and prepare 10 rootstocks for grafting. You will need: 10 healthy rootstock seedlings (mango, avocado, or citrus), a sharp grafting knife, grafting tape, a clean cloth, alcohol for sterilizing, and labels. Work in the morning when it is cool.

Step 1: Select your rootstocks. Choose 10 seedlings that are the correct age and size for your species. For mango, 6-8 months, stem diameter 0.8-1.2 cm. For avocado, 8-12 months, 0.6-1.0 cm. For citrus, 6-10 months, 0.5-0.8 cm. Reject any with pests, disease, or weak growth. Measure stem diameter at 10 cm above soil with a caliper or a string marked against a ruler.

Step 2: Water the seedlings well the day before. On the day, clean the stems with a damp cloth. Sterilize your knife with alcohol. Make a clean cut at 10-15 cm above the soil. For a wedge graft, cut the rootstock stem at a 45-degree angle, then make a vertical slit 2-3 cm deep. For a side graft, make a slanting cut 3-4 cm long. Ensure the cut is smooth and not bruised.

Step 3: Prepare the scion. Collect scion wood from a healthy, high-yielding mother tree of the desired variety. The scion should be the same diameter as the rootstock, with 2-3 buds. Cut the bottom of the scion into a wedge to match the rootstock. Insert the scion into the rootstock so that the cambium layers (the green layer under the bark) meet on at least one side. Wrap tightly with grafting tape. Cover with a plastic bag.

Step 4: Label each grafted plant with the date, rootstock species, and scion variety. Keep in a shaded area for 2-3 weeks. Water lightly. After 3 weeks, check for new growth. Remove the plastic bag and tape after 4-6 weeks. Record your success rate. With practice, you can achieve 80-90% success.

quiz.q: Which rootstock is known for drought tolerance in citrus?
quiz.explanation: Rough lemon (Citrus jambhiri) is widely recognized for its drought tolerance and is a common rootstock in semi-arid areas.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for mango trees in dry areas?
quiz.explanation: Mango trees need 8-10 meters spacing to allow for their large canopy and root system in dry areas.

quiz.q: Which type of mango seed produces multiple seedlings, one of which is a clone?
quiz.explanation: Polyembryonic mango seeds produce multiple seedlings, and one is a genetic clone of the mother tree, making it ideal for rootstock.

quiz.q: How soon should citrus seeds be planted after extraction?
quiz.explanation: Citrus seeds lose viability quickly and should be planted within 24 hours of extraction.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil mix for raising rootstock seedlings in tubes?
options: A) 1 part soil, 1 part sand, 1 part compost
B) 3 parts soil, 2 parts sand, 1 part compost
C) 2 parts soil, 1 part sand, 2 parts compost
D) 1 part soil, 3 parts sand, 1 part compost
quiz.explanation: A mix of 3 parts soil, 2 parts sand, and 1 part compost provides good drainage and nutrients for rootstock seedlings.

quiz.q: When is the best time to transplant rootstocks into nursery beds?
quiz.explanation: Transplanting at the start of the rainy season ensures moist soil and moderate temperatures, reducing transplant shock.

quiz.q: What spacing should be used for rootstock seedlings in a nursery bed?
quiz.explanation: Spacing of 20 cm between plants and 30 cm between rows gives each rootstock enough room for root development.

quiz.q: How long should seedlings be shaded after transplanting into nursery beds?
quiz.explanation: Shading for the first week helps seedlings recover from transplant shock and adapt to full sun.

quiz.q: What is the recommended stem diameter for a mango rootstock ready for grafting?
quiz.explanation: Mango rootstocks are ready for grafting when the stem diameter is 0.8-1.2 cm, about the thickness of a pencil.

quiz.q: Why should you not fertilize rootstocks two weeks before grafting?
options: A) It causes excessive sap flow
B) It makes the stem too hard
quiz.explanation: High nitrogen can cause excessive sap flow, which reduces graft success by interfering with the union.

quiz.q: What is the first step in preparing a rootstock for grafting?
quiz.explanation: Sterilizing the knife prevents introducing diseases into the cut surfaces of the rootstock and scion.

quiz.q: How long should grafting tape be left on after grafting?
quiz.explanation: Grafting tape is typically removed after 4-6 weeks when the graft union has healed.

quiz.q: Which pest can be controlled by spraying soapy water?
quiz.explanation: Soapy water is effective against soft-bodied insects like aphids, whiteflies, and mealybugs.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of liquid soap for pest control?
quiz.explanation: A mix of 1 tablespoon of liquid soap per litre of water is effective and safe for most seedlings.

quiz.q: What disease causes seedlings to collapse at the soil line?
quiz.explanation: Damping-off is a fungal disease that causes seedlings to collapse at the soil line, often due to overwatering.

quiz.q: How can you treat powdery mildew without expensive chemicals?
options: A) Spray with baking soda and soap
quiz.explanation: A mix of 1 tablespoon baking soda and 1 teaspoon liquid soap in 1 litre of water is an effective homemade treatment for powdery mildew.

quiz.q: What is the best way to prevent bacterial diseases like citrus canker?
options: A) Use clean seed and tools
quiz.explanation: Prevention is key: use clean seed, sterilize tools, and remove infected plants to stop the spread of bacterial diseases.

quiz.q: In the hands-on lesson, how many rootstocks should you prepare for grafting?
quiz.explanation: The practical exercise requires selecting and preparing 10 rootstocks for grafting.

quiz.q: What tool is used to measure stem diameter?
quiz.explanation: A caliper is the most accurate tool for measuring stem diameter, though a string marked against a ruler can also work.

quiz.q: What is the expected success rate for grafting with practice?
quiz.explanation: With proper technique and practice, graft success rates of 80-90% are achievable.

quiz.q: Which rootstock is recommended for avocado in dry areas?
quiz.explanation: Duke 7 is known for its drought tolerance and is a recommended avocado rootstock for dry areas.

quiz.q: What is the correct depth to plant an avocado seed?
quiz.explanation: Avocado seeds should be planted pointed end up, about 2 cm deep, to ensure proper germination.

quiz.q: How often should young rootstock seedlings be watered after transplanting?
options: B) Every morning for two weeks
quiz.explanation: Watering every morning for the first two weeks after transplanting helps seedlings establish without water stress.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of mulching around rootstock seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Mulch helps conserve soil moisture and suppress weeds, which is especially important in dry areas.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a healthy rootstock ready for grafting?
quiz.explanation: A healthy rootstock is actively growing, with green leaves and no signs of pests or disease.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see aphids on rootstock seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Soapy water is an effective, low-cost treatment for aphids and other soft-bodied pests.

quiz.q: How can you prevent damping-off in the nursery?
quiz.explanation: Well-drained soil and avoiding overwatering are key to preventing damping-off.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for citrus trees in dry areas?
quiz.explanation: Citrus trees are typically spaced 5-7 meters apart to allow for canopy growth and root development.

quiz.q: When collecting scion wood, what should you look for?
quiz.explanation: Scion wood should come from a healthy, high-yielding mother tree of the desired variety to ensure good fruit quality.

quiz.q: What is the first sign that a graft has taken?
options: A) New growth from the scion
B) Swelling at the graft union
quiz.explanation: New growth from the scion indicates that the graft union has healed and the scion is receiving nutrients.
